Fear of judgment almost kept me silent.But then, I decided to take a leap. I started sharing my journey—my learnings, failures, wins, and even doubts. And guess what? People responded.  Not because I had all the answers, but because they saw a bit of themselves in my posts. We’re all figuring things out, and sometimes, all we need is to know we’re not alone. 🤝 Today, this community has grown to 2⃣0⃣,0⃣0⃣0⃣ amazing people!  And I still can’t believe it!  This isn’t about numbers; it’s about the connections built, the stories exchanged, and the motivation we give each other to keep moving forward.  The best part?       —  .  One thing I’ve always believed in is being approachable. Whether it’s answering questions, guiding someone through a tough concept, or just engaging in thoughtful discussions, I never wanted my presence here to feel distant.  Knowledge grows when shared. If my posts have ever inspired, informed, or encouraged you in any way, that’s my biggest win.  But this journey isn’t just about sharing—it's also about learning. I've gained so much from the brilliant individuals in my network. Whether it's an insightful perspective, a career-changing tip, or simply a different way of looking at things, every post, every conversation, and every comment has helped me grow.  The best part? Learning never stops. I’ve seen people break their self-doubt, land their dream roles, and push their limits, all because of the power of a strong community.  And the best part?     .  There’s so much more to learn, so many more people to uplift, and endless opportunities ahead.  To everyone who has liked, commented, shared, or even just read my posts— !  You make this journey worthwhile. Your support and engagement have made this space more meaningful, and I genuinely appreciate every interaction. New things coming my way make me feel a lot anxious.I received an email stating this to seek help into such scenarios.I felt that everyone going through the same situation should know this. We sometimes overthink and mess up things or hype it a lot and later realize it was a piece of cake.I also sometimes become anxious about new things. Through my experiences I felt we can handle these feelings in the following way.Research:Do some research about incoming opportunities beforehand. Try to gather as much information as possible, so that you'll know what it is going to be already.Seek Guidance:Ask about it to your seniors who already have gone through it. Your mentors can also help you. Discuss with your friends, you'll get to know you're not alone in this.Prepare and Plan:Plan your stuff according to gathered information. Preparing in advance can reduce uncertainty and boost your confidence.Take Small Steps:Break down new tasks or challenges into smaller, manageable steps. This can make them feel less overwhelming.Focus on the Positive:Remind yourself of past successes when you overcame challenges. Trust in your ability to handle new situations.Stay Resilient:If you fear a lot about failure, then already train your mind to ask a question what I'll do if I fail?Facing every opportunity to win but always being resilient to failures, being well prepared, having a plan and learning mindset is the key. What you need to do for it. And get started working on it. Because your actions are revealing your true motivations!!M. Over the past 4 months, I’ve been exploring how to combine emotion with intelligence in an AI solution. What many see as isolating, I see as an opportunity for connection and collaboration. My focus has been on AI companions for Carnatic music—crafting a digital personality, bringing it to life through a persona agent, LLMs with RAG, and always centering on the “what’s in it for me” for users.

Key takeaways from my exploration so far:

1) Some may resist the reality that AI is here to stay, but the wise approach is to guide its potential toward positive outcomes.

2) Go beyond listening—uncover user needs they may not even realize themselves.

3) Success in tech-driven projects hinges on bridging the gap between domain experts and technologists, fostering diverse teams that respect and learn from each other.

4) Creating human-centric solutions often means embracing advanced tech. This journey taught me to overcome mental barriers and harness the synergy of design, expertise, and technology for impactful innovation.

From Dream to Reality: The Changing Landscape of IT Careers 
As a child, I used to believe that working in IT was the ultimate dream—high-paying, respected, and something every college student aspired to. And for years, it was true. The tech industry flourished, companies expanded, and opportunities were everywhere.
Fast forward to today, after nearly 5 years in this field, I see a shift. While many still aim to break into IT, an increasing number of professionals now talk about leaving it behind. I hear colleagues expressing their desire to start a business in their hometowns, chasing independence and stability. On the other side, companies are laying off employees in bulk, making job security a growing concern.
So, what changed? Is it the evolving job market, the pressure of corporate life, or the realization that passion lies elsewhere?
I’d love to hear your thoughts. Are you still chasing an IT dream, or are you looking for a way out?

As new opportunities on the horizon, I must admit that anxiety can be a debilitating companion. Receiving guidance from a trusted source has been invaluable in navigating these situations. It's essential to share this insight with others who may be facing similar challenges.

To mitigate anxiety and maximize success, consider the following strategies:

Research is key: Gather as much information as possible before diving into new opportunities. This foresight will enable you to better understand what lies ahead.

Seek guidance from seasoned professionals or mentors. They can offer valuable insights and reassurance that others may not be able to provide.

Plan and prepare: Utilize the knowledge gathered during research to create a roadmap for success. This proactive approach will not only reduce uncertainty but also bolster confidence.

Break down daunting tasks into manageable steps. By doing so, you'll be better equipped to tackle new challenges without feeling overwhelmed.

Focus on past successes: When faced with anxiety about new situations, reflect on your previous accomplishments and the skills that helped you overcome obstacles.

Cultivate resilience: Instead of fearing failure, prepare yourself for its possibility by asking "what if I fail?" Develop a growth mindset and focus on being well-prepared, having a plan, and learning from failures.

Your actions are a reflection of your priorities. If you express commitment to something but fail to take action, it's time to reassess your motivations and true desires. Take an honest look at yourself and make the necessary adjustments to achieve your goals.

The Landscape of IT Careers: A Shift in Aspirations and Reality

As a child, I once held IT as the pinnacle of career aspirations – renowned for its prestige, lucrative compensation, and widespread opportunities. This narrative held true for years, with the tech industry experiencing rapid growth, companies expanding their reach, and job prospects abound.

However, nearly five years into my own IT career, I have observed a significant transformation. Many professionals are now openly discussing their desire to transition away from this field. I've spoken with colleagues who aspire to leave behind the corporate world and establish a business in their hometowns, driven by a desire for independence and stability. Concurrently, companies are significantly reducing staff, casting doubt on job security.
So, what has precipitated this shift? Is it the evolving job market, the pressures of corporate life, or the realization that individual passions lie elsewhere?

I'd appreciate your insights. Are you still pursuing an IT career, or are you seeking alternative paths?

As new opportunities and challenges emerge, I've found myself grappling with feelings of anxiety. Recently, I received guidance on navigating these situations, which I'd like to share with others who may be facing similar concerns. It's easy to overthink and magnify the significance of uncertain events, only to realize later that they were manageable and not as daunting as initially perceived.

To mitigate such anxiety, I recommend the following strategies:

Research: Proactively gather information about incoming opportunities before diving in. This will help you better understand what to expect and reduce uncertainty.

Seek Guidance: Reach out to experienced professionals who have navigated similar situations. Your seniors, mentors, or friends can offer valuable insights and reassurance that you're not alone.

Prepare and Plan: Utilize the knowledge gathered through research to create a plan of action. This will help boost your confidence and prepare you for potential outcomes.

Take Small Steps: Break down complex tasks into smaller, manageable steps. By doing so, you'll make them feel less overwhelming and more achievable.

Focus on the Positive: Reflect on past successes and remind yourself of your ability to overcome challenges. Trust in your capacity to handle new situations and bounce back from setbacks.

Stay Resilient: Cultivate a mindset that views failure as an opportunity for growth. Train yourself to ask, "What would I do if I failed?" and focus on learning and adaptation rather than fear of defeat. This resilience is key to successfully navigating new challenges.

In the face of uncertainty, it's essential to be honest with yourself about what you truly want and need. If your actions don't align with your priorities, it's time for a self-reflection. Your actions reveal your true motivations and desires; take ownership of them and start working towards making them a reality.

The Evolution of IT Careers: Navigating the Changing Landscape

As a child, I once viewed working in IT as the epitome of success – financially rewarding, respected, and an aspiration for many aspiring professionals. For years, this vision held true, with the tech industry experiencing rapid growth, companies expanding, and opportunities abound.
However, nearly 5 years into my own IT career, I have observed a significant shift. The notion of breaking into this field has become increasingly challenging, as I hear colleagues expressing a desire to transition towards entrepreneurship or establish their own businesses in their hometowns, driven by the pursuit of independence and stability.
Conversely, companies are laying off employees in bulk, casting a shadow over job security. This paradox raises an intriguing question: what has led to this transformation? Is it the evolving nature of the job market, the pressures of corporate life, or the realization that personal passions lie elsewhere?
I'd appreciate your insights on this topic. Are you still pursuing a career in IT, or are you exploring alternative paths? Your thoughts and experiences can provide valuable context for our collective understanding of the changing landscape.

As I prepare for the next chapter in my professional journey, I've come to realize that anxiety can be a formidable obstacle. Fortunately, having a trusted advisor has been instrumental in helping me navigate uncertain situations. I'd like to share this valuable insight with fellow professionals who may be facing similar challenges.

To effectively manage anxiety and optimize success, consider adopting the following strategies:

Investing in research is crucial: Gathering as much information as possible prior to embarking on new opportunities will enable you to make more informed decisions and gain a deeper understanding of what lies ahead.

Seek guidance from seasoned experts or mentors who can offer unique perspectives and reassurance. Their insights can provide invaluable support during times of uncertainty.

Developing a comprehensive plan is essential: Utilizing the knowledge gathered through research, create a roadmap for success that prioritizes proactive planning and preparation. This approach will not only alleviate uncertainty but also foster confidence.

Breaking down daunting tasks into manageable components is vital to overcoming anxiety. By doing so, you can effectively tackle new challenges without feeling overwhelmed or intimidated.

Reflecting on past successes and accomplishments can be a powerful tool in combating anxiety related to new situations. Focus on the skills that helped you overcome obstacles and leverage those strengths to inform your future endeavors.

Cultivating resilience is also essential: Rather than fear failure, prepare yourself for its possibility by considering alternative scenarios. Adopt a growth mindset, focus on being well-prepared, having a plan, and learning from failures – this will help you build confidence and navigate uncertainty with greater ease.

Your actions serve as a reflection of your priorities, so it's essential to be honest about your motivations and true desires. Take an introspective look at yourself and make necessary adjustments to align with your goals and aspirations.

Many professionals are now openly expressing their desire to transition away from this field, driven by a pursuit of autonomy and stability. I've spoken with colleagues who aspire to leave behind the corporate world and establish a business in their hometowns, seeking a more independent existence.

Concurrently, companies are significantly reducing staff, casting doubt on job security and exacerbating concerns about career stability. So, what has precipitated this shift? Is it the evolving nature of the job market, the pressures of corporate life, or the realization that individual passions lie elsewhere?

I'd appreciate your insights. Are you still committed to pursuing an IT career, or are you exploring alternative paths that align with your personal aspirations and values?

The Evolution of IT Careers: A Changing Landscape

My perception of the IT industry as an ideal career path has undergone a significant transformation over the years. As a child, I believed that working in IT would be the ultimate aspiration – offering high remuneration, respect, and opportunities for every college graduate. Unfortunately, this narrative has not held true in recent times.

In fact, I've noticed a marked shift in the past five years. While many individuals still aspire to break into the field, an increasing number of professionals are considering alternative paths. Some colleagues have expressed a desire to start their own businesses in their hometowns, driven by a quest for independence and stability. Conversely, companies are laying off employees on a large scale, casting doubt on job security.
So, what has contributed to this shift? Is it the dynamic nature of the job market, the pressures of corporate life, or the realization that true passion lies elsewhere?
I'd appreciate hearing your perspectives on this topic. Are you still pursuing an IT career, or are you exploring options for a career transition?

As I navigate the complexities of emerging opportunities and challenges, I've come to realize that anxiety can be a pervasive obstacle. Recently, I had the privilege of receiving valuable guidance on managing these feelings, which I'd like to share with others who may be grappling with similar concerns.

It's easy to get caught up in overthinking and magnifying the significance of uncertain events, only to discover later that they were manageable and not as daunting as initially perceived. To mitigate this anxiety, I've found several strategies to be highly effective:

Proactively gathering information about incoming opportunities through research can provide a clear understanding of what to expect, thereby reducing uncertainty.

Seeking guidance from experienced professionals who have navigated similar situations can offer valuable insights and reassurance that you're not alone in your journey. Reaching out to seniors, mentors, or friends can be an excellent way to tap into their expertise and gain new perspectives.

Preparing and planning for potential outcomes by utilizing the knowledge gathered through research can significantly boost confidence and help prepare one for various scenarios.

Breaking down complex tasks into smaller, manageable steps can make them feel less overwhelming and more achievable. By doing so, you'll be able to tackle seemingly insurmountable challenges with greater ease.

Focusing on past successes and reminding yourself of your ability to overcome challenges can instill a sense of confidence in the face of uncertainty. Reflecting on these experiences can help you trust in your capacity to handle new situations and bounce back from setbacks.

Cultivating a growth mindset by viewing failure as an opportunity for growth rather than fear of defeat is essential for successfully navigating new challenges. By asking yourself, "What would I do if I failed?", and focusing on learning and adaptation rather than fear, you'll be better equipped to handle uncertainty with resilience.

It's equally important to take ownership of your actions and prioritize what truly matters to you. If your actions don't align with your priorities, it's time for self-reflection. By being honest with yourself about your true desires and needs, you can create a clear path forward and make progress towards making them a reality.

In my formative years, I once viewed an IT career as a pinnacle of success - financially rewarding, prestigious, and a coveted aspiration among aspiring professionals. I'm pleased to announce the publication of my latest research, which represents a significant advancement in motion detection capabilities by integrating cutting-edge technologies such as real-time tracking and object recognition. The result is a pioneering Smart Detectors System (SDS) that not only detects movement but also identifies objects in real-time with unparalleled precision.

The system's sensor fusion capabilities are its most distinctive feature. As an object approaches the sensor, accuracy increases while signal intensity diminishes if it is at a distance. This results in real-time intelligence and adaptability to complex scenarios, where threat levels can vary greatly.

One of the SDS's notable attributes is its 90-degree rotation mechanism, which introduces an interactive layer when motion is detected. This characteristic renders our system particularly well-suited for applications such as automated doors, security systems, and robotics. By leveraging this technology, it is possible to create innovative solutions in various real-world contexts.

The Real-Time, Adaptive System (RTAS) stands out for its exceptional performance in areas like home security, automation, and futuristic robotics. The Paradox of Expectations in the IT Industry: A Reality Check

As I reflect on my own IT career, which has spanned nearly five years, I am struck by the disparity between industry expectations and the harsh realities that many professionals are now confronting. The notion of IT as a prestigious field with limitless opportunities for growth and success has persisted for decades, despite the tech industry's growing global presence.

However, recent conversations with colleagues have revealed a surprising trend: many individuals are seeking to transition out of the corporate world and establish their own businesses, driven by a desire for autonomy, stability, and a more meaningful connection between work and personal values. At the same time, companies are reducing staff at an alarming rate, casting a shadow of uncertainty over job security and exacerbating concerns about career stability.

So, what is driving this shift? Is it the rapid evolution of the job market, the pressures of modern corporate life, or the growing realization that individual passions lie outside the realm of traditional IT roles? I would love to hear your thoughts on this topic. Are you still committed to pursuing a career in IT, or are you exploring alternative paths that align with your unique aspirations and values?

As I prepare to embark on new endeavors, I've found that anxiety can be a formidable obstacle. Fortunately, having access to trusted guidance has been instrumental in helping me navigate these uncertain times. Sharing this experience with others who may be facing similar challenges is essential to creating a supportive community.

To effectively manage anxiety and capitalize on success, consider implementing the following strategies:

Cultivating strategic foresight: Gathering extensive information before diving into new opportunities can provide a critical advantage. This proactive approach will enable you to better grasp the complexities involved and make informed decisions.

Seeking mentorship from seasoned professionals or industry experts: Leveraging their collective wisdom and expertise can offer invaluable insights, reassurance, and perspective that may not be readily available through self-directed efforts.

Developing a comprehensive plan: Utilizing gathered knowledge to create a roadmap for success will not only reduce uncertainty but also enhance confidence and preparedness.

Breaking down daunting tasks into manageable components: By doing so, you'll be better equipped to tackle new challenges with clarity and determination, rather than feeling overwhelmed by the magnitude of the task.

Reflecting on past achievements: When faced with anxiety about new situations, it's essential to draw upon your previous successes and the skills that facilitated them. This will help you identify areas of strength and build confidence in your ability to overcome obstacles.

Embracing resilience: Rather than fearing failure, prepare yourself for its possibility by asking "what if I fail?" Develop a growth mindset, focusing on being well-prepared, having a plan, and learning from failures.

Your actions are a reflection of your priorities. If you express commitment to something but fail to take action, it's crucial to reassess your motivations and true desires. Take an honest look at yourself and make the necessary adjustments to align with your goals and values.

The Evolution of IT Careers: A Shift in Aspirations and Reality

In my formative years, I was captivated by the allure of IT as a premier career destination – characterized by its prestige, financial rewards, and extensive job opportunities. This perception held sway for an extended period, coinciding with the rapid expansion of the tech industry, widespread corporate growth, and abundant employment prospects.

Notably, over five years into my own professional journey in IT, I have observed a profound paradigm shift. Increasingly, I am encountering individuals who are vocally expressing their intent to depart from this field. Personal conversations with colleagues have revealed a growing desire among professionals to break away from the corporate landscape and establish entrepreneurial ventures in their local communities, driven by a quest for autonomy and stability.

Concurrently, I have witnessed significant reductions in staffing levels within companies, casting uncertainty over job security. So, what has precipitated this seismic shift? Is it a response to changes in the market, the pressures of corporate life, or the recognition that individual passions lie outside the realm of IT?

I would greatly appreciate your insights on this matter. Are you still pursuing an IT career, or are you considering alternative paths?

As I navigate the ever-evolving landscape of opportunities and challenges, I've come to realize that uncertainty can be a formidable obstacle. Recently, I was fortunate enough to receive valuable guidance on managing anxiety in the face of ambiguity, which I'd like to share with others who may be facing similar concerns.

It's easy to get caught up in overthinking and magnifying the significance of uncertain events, only to discover later that they were manageable and not as daunting as initially perceived. To mitigate such anxiety, I've found the following strategies to be particularly effective:

Conduct thorough research: Proactively gathering information about incoming opportunities can help demystify uncertainty and reduce feelings of unease.

Seek expert guidance: Reaching out to experienced professionals who have navigated similar situations can provide invaluable insights and reassurance that you're not alone in your journey.

Develop a plan: Leveraging the knowledge gained through research, create a comprehensive plan of action that empowers confidence and prepares you for potential outcomes.

Break tasks into manageable steps: By dissecting complex challenges into smaller, more achievable components, you'll be able to tackle them with greater ease and reduce feelings of overwhelm.

Focus on past successes: Reflecting on your past achievements can help reinforce your capacity for resilience and remind you that you're equipped to handle new situations. Cultivate a growth mindset by trusting in your ability to adapt and learn from setbacks.

Maintain a resilient mindset: View failure as an opportunity for growth, rather than defeat. Ask yourself "what would I do if I failed?" and focus on learning and adaptation rather than fear of failure. This resilience is essential for successfully navigating new challenges.

Be honest with yourself about your priorities: Take the time to reflect on what truly drives you and what you want to achieve. If your actions don't align with your goals, it's essential to re-evaluate and make necessary adjustments. Your actions reveal your true motivations and desires; take ownership of them and start working towards making them a reality.

Together, let's cultivate growth, collaboration, and empowerment. By supporting one another, we can rise above uncertainty and achieve our goals as a cohesive unit. #GrowthMindset #Collaboration #Empowerment #Innovation #RiseTogether

The IT Profession's Evolving Landscape: Shifting Priorities and Realities

As a child, I was drawn to the IT industry as a pinnacle of professional aspiration - characterized by its prestige, financial rewards, and extensive opportunities. This narrative persisted for years, with the tech sector experiencing exponential growth, companies expanding globally, and job prospects seeming virtually limitless.

However, nearly five years into my own IT career, I've observed a profound shift in the industry's dynamics. Many professionals are now openly expressing their desire to transition away from this field. I've engaged in discussions with colleagues who aspire to leave behind the corporate environment and establish a business in their hometowns, driven by a craving for autonomy, stability, and a better work-life balance. Concurrently, companies are significantly reducing staff, casting doubt on job security and forcing professionals to reassess their career goals.
The question remains: what is driving this shift? Is it the changing nature of the job market, the pressures of corporate life, or the realization that individual passions and interests lie outside the IT sector?

I'd appreciate your insights. Are you currently pursuing an IT career, or are you exploring alternative paths and options to find greater fulfillment and stability in your professional endeavors?

As I navigate the dynamic landscape of emerging opportunities and challenges, I've come to appreciate the importance of managing anxiety. Recently, I was fortunate to receive insightful guidance on mitigating these feelings, which I'd like to share with others who may be struggling with similar concerns.

It's easy to become mired in overthinking and amplifying the significance of uncertain events, only to discover later that they were more manageable than initially perceived. To overcome this anxiety, I've found several strategies to be highly effective:

Conducting thorough research on incoming opportunities can provide a clear understanding of what to expect, thereby reducing uncertainty and uncertainty-driven stress.

Seeking guidance from experienced professionals who have navigated similar situations can offer valuable insights and reassurance that you're not alone in your journey. Leveraging the expertise of seniors, mentors, or friends can be an excellent way to tap into their knowledge and gain new perspectives.

Developing a plan for potential outcomes by utilizing the knowledge gathered through research can significantly boost confidence and help prepare one for various scenarios. This proactive approach can empower individuals to tackle complex challenges with greater ease.

Breaking down complex tasks into smaller, manageable steps can make them feel less overwhelming and more achievable. By doing so, you'll be able to tackle seemingly insurmountable challenges with greater resilience.

Focusing on past successes and reminding yourself of your ability to overcome challenges can instill a sense of confidence in the face of uncertainty. Reflecting on these experiences can help you trust in your capacity to handle new situations and bounce back from setbacks.

Cultivating a growth mindset by viewing failure as an opportunity for growth rather than fear of defeat is essential for successfully navigating new challenges. By asking yourself, "What would I do if I failed?", and focusing on learning and adaptation rather than fear, you'll be better equipped to handle uncertainty with resilience.

It's equally important to take ownership of your actions and prioritize what truly matters to you. If your actions don't align with your priorities, it's time for self-reflection. By being honest with yourself about your true desires and needs, you can create a clear path forward and make progress towards making them a reality.

Is it the changing nature of the job market, the pressures of corporate existence, or the realization that personal passions and values lie outside the traditional IT sector?
I'd appreciate your insights on this topic. Are you still pursuing a career in IT, or are you exploring alternative paths? However, recent conversations with peers have revealed a striking paradox: numerous individuals are seeking to transition out of the corporate realm and establish their own ventures, driven by a desire for independence, stability, and a more authentic alignment between professional pursuits and personal values. Concurrently, companies are reducing staff at an alarming rate, casting a shadow of uncertainty over job security and exacerbating concerns about career stability.

This juxtaposition raises fundamental questions: what is driving this shift away from traditional IT roles? Is it the dynamic nature of the job market, the pressures of modern corporate life, or the growing realization that individual passions lie beyond the scope of conventional IT careers? Last night I was riding through San Francisco in a Waymo with Alex Lau (author of Keep Calm, Code On), passing giant AI billboards promising to automate us out of jobs.

Naturally the conversation turned to the future of software engineers.

Neither of us claims to know the answer. But one thing is clear: the job is changing faster than most people realize.

I’ve started noticing a few predictable levels of AI leverage developers move through. Most people are stuck at level one.

The interesting opportunities are in the levels beyond that.

Here’s what those look like.

I was demoing an AI agent (𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘢 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘧𝘭𝘰𝘸 𝘣𝘶𝘵, 𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘢𝘵𝘰) — that broke at the worst possible time.

Our CEO asked it to find influencers in our database that charged less than $1000 per post.

No results.

I had tried this scenario so many times before demo day.

What happened?!

When I inspected the logs, I saw our agent was sometimes parsing 1K as $1 or $10 instead of $1000 😅

So the agent searched the database and confidently concluded:

🤖 “𝘕𝘰 𝘪𝘯𝘧𝘭𝘶𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘥.”

A tiny interpretation mistake that completely broke the outcome.

This is something I’ve noticed a lot building AI agents:

They fail in subtle, unexpected ways like unit conversions, formatting quirks and edge cases you don't think about.

In our case, the fix wasn’t fancy. 

We added a regex parser to extract the price and compare it against what the AI produced. LLM observability tools like Langsmith allowed us to track these differences and determine if tweaks to our system prompt improved accuracy.

Not sexy.

At Parsity, we’ve been against AI tool use while students are learning to code.

This was not an easy decision and I'd be lying if I said I was 100% sure that this was the right move.

Emerging research (and what we see in practice) supports our position:

• 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 (𝗺𝗶𝘀)𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴: Students finish tasks without building real mental models
• 𝗗𝗲𝗯𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: Fewer mistakes == fewer chances to learn how systems actually break
• 𝗟𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗵𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻: Reading AI output != knowing how to write or fix it yourself
• 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: Performance drops when the AI “exoskeleton” is removed

Yes, AI can boost short-term productivity.
But learning to code was never about speed. It’s about building the brain.

That’s why our students learn fundamentals first.

AI comes later. Once they can evaluate, debug, and supervise it.

We’re not anti-AI.
We’re pro-skill formation.

If you’re using AI to write your code, here’s something you should know.

If you are:

• using AI to generate production code
• using AI to generate the tests
• using AI to validate its own output
• and then shipping it

Then you are MORE likely than a human to ship bugs and vulnerabilities.

Specifically, you are more likely than a human to:

• Introduce security vulnerabilities (~20-25% higher likelihood)
• Ship critical or major bugs (≈1.5–1.7× more per PR)
• Miss edge cases and failure paths in tests
• Over-test happy paths and under-test bad inputs
• Have “clean” builds that hide production risks

AI-written tests are less likely to test edge cases and over-use mocks.

LGTM! 😅

This doesn’t mean “don’t use AI.”

It means 100% AI-generated systems should make you pause and consider the risks.

Output scales fast. Judgment and maintenance won't.

Here are 4 mistakes I made when building agents:
   
❌ 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲
✅ If the steps are deterministic and predictable, 𝗮 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.
Agents make sense when planning, exploration, or autonomy are required.

❌ 𝗣𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 (𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴) 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁
✅ Good agents get the right information at the right moment. Context should be intentional and managed, not a full memory dump.

❌ 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁 (𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿)𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴
✅ Clear structure, consistent formatting, and a few concrete examples outperform clever wording.

❌ 𝗨𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸
✅ Different tasks benefit from different models.
Routing, extraction, and classification don’t need heavyweight reasoning.

𝟭. 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝘁𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗽𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴

We were told output would explode. Instead, we got more bugs, more rewrites, and more pressure to ship faster without better systems in place.

𝟯. 𝗝𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗴𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗲𝘇𝗲𝗱

𝟭. 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝘁𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗽𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗽𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝘆𝘂𝗽, 𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁𝘀)

AI didn’t fail this year.
 
It failed expectations.
 
No mass job extinction. No solo unicorn founders. No “prompt your way to riches.”
 
Reality was less marketable:

• uneven usefulness
• uneven adoption
• a widening gap between people who know how to think and people hoping AI will think for them
 
Developers felt this first.
 
AI raised expectations. Output increased. So did bugs. We all felt a historic number of outages.
 
𝗠𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

1. 𝘈𝘐 𝘴𝘦𝘵𝘵𝘭𝘦𝘴 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘯𝘧𝘳𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦.
 
Agents improve in reliability and scope. Teams stop chasing novelty and start standardizing workflows. Excitement fades. Usefulness increases.
 
Agent design patterns solidify the same way frameworks and cloud architectures eventually did.
 
2. 𝘓𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘴 𝘴𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘦
 
Learners reach for AI as a teacher first. Tutorials lose relevance because the fastest path to understanding becomes interactive and contextual.

I also don't believe this will work. Hallucinations and overly general learning paths frustrate users moving past the beginner stage.

People rediscover mentorship and opt for more human experiences.
 
3. 𝘛𝘦𝘤𝘩 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘦𝘸𝘴 𝘨𝘦𝘵... 𝘥𝘪𝘧𝘧𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘵

What you’ll be able to build in ~6–8 weeks (1–2 hrs/night): a docs Q&A bot for your repo, a customer-support search tool, or a summarizer that plugs into your app. 

Real projects, not demo toys.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗵:
• 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁: tokens, embeddings, vectors, context window, latency/cost. You don’t need PhD math - just enough to reason about tradeoffs.
• 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗮 𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿: Next.js + Vercel AI SDK (or OpenAI/Anthropic SDK). One route, one prompt, stream the response. Push to prod day 1.

• 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲/𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀: log tokens and latency per request. Set monthly caps.
• 𝗨𝗽𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗫: add tool/function calling for structured outputs, retries with fallbacks, and guardrails for edge cases.

I’m testing a new app I built that can draft posts in my voice, suggest relevant lead magnets, and pull in examples from past content. It uses tool-calling, RAG, and a vector index of 1,000+ of my posts to get close to how I actually write.

Why share this? Because “AI for content” doesn’t have to be fluff. Here’s a practical example and how I got it working.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀:

• 𝗜𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝘆 𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲: It retrieves similar posts from my archive and mirrors tone, length, and structure.
• 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲: It can suggest relevant resources (like an AI lead magnet) and drop the right links.
• 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗼𝗻-𝗺𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲: It pulls my business context (programs, voice, audience) before it writes, so it’s not guessing.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 (𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹):

• Stack: TypeScript + Next.js + OpenAI function/tool-calling + a vector database for retrieval + Vercel AI SDK.
• RAG: I chunked ~1,000 posts, embedded them, and use semantic search to retrieve 5–10 examples as grounding before it drafts.
• Tool-calling orchestration:
• Tool A fetches brand/business context (voice, audience, programs).
• Tool B retrieves similar writing samples to match style.
• Tool C searches my resource library to recommend the right lead magnet.
• Guardrails:
• Schema validation for structured outputs (titles, hooks, bullets).
• Unit tests with an LLM-as-judge to catch regressions in tone and truthiness.
• Caching on prompt prefixes to keep latency/cost under control.
• Human-in-the-loop: I still review, tighten, and fact-check. It’s a co-writer, not a replacement.

If you’re curious about building this kind of thing, start with a small RAG pipeline and add tool-calling later. Keep it boring: get retrieval working reliably, then layer on features like resource suggestions and schema’d outputs.

During an internship for Parsity students, we had to SSH into a server instance on AWS to figure out how to deploy some code that our grads had been working on.

I realized how often I've had to do tasks like this to troubleshoot issues on remote servers. It can be stressful. 

𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰 𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀, 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗳𝘂𝗹.

Our grads jumped into this codebase made by contractors who we have no contact with.

Ruh roh.

𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗿. Turns out, the original developer would SSH into the box, pull down the code from GitHub and then restart the server manually.

No judgment... except of course I am.

𝚌𝚊𝚝 ~/.𝚋𝚊𝚜𝚑_𝚑𝚒𝚜𝚝𝚘𝚛𝚢

Now I could see the evil genius at work here and why our app was crashing. I made a code change on the fly and the work our grads created was now LIVE.

𝘖𝘩 𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘩, 𝘥𝘰𝘯'𝘵 𝘥𝘦𝘱𝘭𝘰𝘺 𝘰𝘯 𝘍𝘳𝘪𝘥𝘢𝘺𝘴.

𝗧𝗟𝗗𝗥; learn some terminal commands. Learn some vim. It won't suck and you'll look way cooler when you're at the coffee shop working on that SAAS app.

What is the 1 thing that separates bootcamp grads who get hired vs those who don’t? 

I’ve thought about this a lot, especially as I’m now the owner of a coding bootcamp (𝘸𝘦 𝘥𝘰𝘯'𝘵 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘮 𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩) Parsity.

I’ve seen too many success stories (and failures) from unlikely people. 

- The guy who struggled to memorize how to complete a for-loop? Hired before the program ended. 
- The woman with a CS degree? Nearly a year and 100s of applications for her to get a break. 

There is very little rhyme, reason or “hack” I can confidently suggest. 

Except this: 

𝗚𝗿𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲. 

The surest way towards failure is to quit. 

Most people will choose this route. 

𝗗𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗵𝘆. Build stuff or do LeetCode or Odin Project. Do something where your hands are on a keyboard making code do stuff. 
𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀? Maybe work on that. 
𝗚𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴? Good. Work on that. 

Good luck out there!

Did you hear what happened with Claude Code recently?

Props to them for making this public.

BUT - do you see the problem here?

These tools are complete black-boxes with non-deterministic outputs. Code quality is subjective and in order to know what's bad - you first need to know what's good.

If you're an early career developer, I'd take this as a cautionary tale and be careful before you outsource your career to the latest AI tool.

What did I miss?

You're going to hate to hear this but... 

There are people less qualified than you who are getting hired faster. 

LinkedIn is a social media site pretending to be a job site. 

On one end you have recruiters trying to find candidates in a tidal wave of AI produced slop. 

On the other end you have qualified candidates who are basically invisible to the algorithm.

So, who's winning here? (hint: not you)

𝗦𝗼 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗮 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗹𝘂𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗿? I mean, it's not the worst idea 😅.

Anyone experienced this shift? Or is this a skillz issue?

The job search can feel unrewarding, draining and shake what little confidence you have in yourself.

Last night at Parsity we had serial guest speaker Brian Schuster share some practical, no-nonsense on the job search which he just went through.

Here's the thing though: it’s a game of both skill and chance.

𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 “𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹”.

Rejection is rarely personal, it’s an inevitable consequence of many factors:

- Resume quality is subjective (ask 5 people to look at your resume and get 5 different opinions)
- Some companies hire internal candidates but open roles to the public
- Engineering interviews can be biased in favor of a specific answer even when presented with working (or even better) alternatives

So what does this mean?

Expect failure and learn from it.

Try your hardest not to take it personally.Whatever you do, please do not stop playing the game.

You only have to win once.

At some point, you need to take off the training wheels.

You’re going to learn a hell of a lot more from:

• getting stuck
• reading the documentation
• realizing the docs suck
• scouring Stack Overflow
• getting rate limited on ChatGPT
• throwing everything at the wall
• finally figuring it out
• wanting to share your excitement and realizing your non-coding friends don't care 😑

as opposed to:

....typing what another person has typed.

Just 2 years ago we were shocked that auto-complete tools like GitHub co-pilot were finishing functions for us. 

Now we have Chet in marketing vibe coding his SAAS app over the weekend.

Unfortunately, too many software developers don’t realize the game has changed beyond using code-gen tools like Cursor and Claude.

Tech interviews are weird.

Just this week at Parsity, we saw:

• One student doing a 𝟲-𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 that included recruiter chats, assessments, team interviews, and a CEO conversation. NO coding rounds.
• Another juggling 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘀 with exclusively LeetCode-style questions.
• Another prepping for a 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱-𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘆 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗽 with front end challenge.

Interviews don’t have a single format.

Some look like algorithm gauntlets.
Some are behavioral-heavy and have 0 coding involved.
Some are just about whether you can clearly explain your past work.

If you’re preparing for interviews, don’t fall into the trap of thinking it’s only about LeetCode or only about system design.

Instead:

• Prepare for the most obvious 𝗯𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (tell me about a time…)

• And expect curveballs: panels, assessments, or multiple informal chats

Most importantly, just ask.

Use Glassdoor, TeamBlind and your recruiter so you're not guessing.

The job search can feel unrewarding, draining and shake what little confidence you have in yourself.

It’s a game of skill and chance.

You can be absolutely qualified and still “fail”.

Rejection is rarely personal, it’s an inevitable consequence of many factors:

- 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 (ask 5 people to look at your resume and get 5 different opinions)
- 𝗦𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 but open roles to the public with 0 intention of hiring
- 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 in favor of a specific answer even when presented with working (or even better) alternatives

So what does this mean?

𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝘁.

Try your hardest not to take it personally.

Whatever you do, please do not stop playing the game.

You only have to win once.

Are we done with vibe coding yet?

Too many software developers are obsessed with the surface layer when it comes to using AI. 

The fun stuff is just a layer below.

Over the last 12 months I've been using AI in production apps which has not only been fun, but has also significantly increased interest in my profile 😉.

I won't call these tips or tricks. There aren't many standards when it comes to using these tools so I'll just share how I'm working with them:

1. 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: LLMs can return the kind of structured data we expect in software development if you provide a schema. OpenAI supports this OOTB with Zod.
2.  𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀: A small tweak to a prompt can break things fast. Using an LLM-as-a-judge in a unit test for a function that relies on an AI response has alerted me to breaking changes. I run these tests daily or before deploying since they are not free.
3.  𝗟𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴: OpenAI caches prompts when the prefixes are the same. Keeping dynamic content at the end of a prompt saves time and a little bit of money.
4. 𝗦𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘆: I'm done writing complicated parsing logic. I throw all the HTML from a scraping job to an LLM and it gives me a structured response.

There's so much more I'm exploring and experimenting with at work and at home including RAG, fine-tuning and agents. 

It's a fun time to be a software developer.

I’ve spoken with over 500 developers in the last 12 months. I won’t be doing any more 15 minute chats in the foreseeable future.

But the truth is, most beginners ask the same 3 questions:

𝙒𝙝𝙖𝙩’𝙨 𝙬𝙧𝙤𝙣𝙜 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝 𝙢𝙮 𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙪𝙢𝙚?

𝙃𝙤𝙬 𝙙𝙤 𝙄 𝙜𝙚𝙩 𝙝𝙞𝙧𝙚𝙙?

So I want to answer them for free:

𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗯𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀. Remove any mention of junior or aspiring and use this framework: did [x] using [y] which led to [z]. Think from the recruiter’s perspective. Do you sound like a risk to hire? Make yourself less risky and don’t tell them everything. Why do they need to know your last job was at a french fry shop? Lead with your developer experience or technical projects.

𝗦𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗻𝗲𝘄 or keep your skills sharp if you’re not working. Really, they should be enjoyable. They’re an alternative to grinding away at toy problems and expose you to challenges which you can give yourself. Want to understand how to implement role-based authentication or get your hands dirty with serverless? Build it out. Also follow John Crickett, he has a ton of cool projects to make.

Now here’s the hard part and the truth no one wants to hear: 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝘂𝗰𝗸. 

If there is one trait that I see in successful grads, it is their consistency. They just didn’t stop. They outlasted their fears, insecurities and the fear mongers. They changed what didn’t work and picked a strategy. 

Mass apply or network or do both. Then don’t stop.

If you’re a little shy try this:

1. Open up Leetcode or whatever tool you’re using to study problems (also... stop with the LeetCode already for the love of Bob)
2. Set the timer on your phone for 30 - 45 mins
3. Open up a video recording tool and explain your thought process and code as you type
4. Watch it later and cringe a bit
5. Repeat until you cringe less

You’re not in school anymore. 

No one is chasing you. You have to own your learning process or you will get eaten alive.

You need to:
• Filter resources instead of binging every tutorial
• Actually 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥 the documentation
• Ask better questions, especially when stuck
• Practice spaced repetition and revisit concepts over time
• Write down what you don’t understand, not just what you do

If you want a method, here’s a good one:

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗲𝘆𝗻𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲
1. Pick a topic (e.g. closures, promises, the call stack)
2. Try to explain it in simple terms
3. Identify what you can’t explain
4. Go back, learn it again, then re-explain it

At Parsity we take it a step further and have students do something they hate: explain these concepts over video 😅.

This is the secret sauce: doing uncomfortable stuff that forces your growth.

A 4 step guide to creating a side project when you don't know what the f*ck to build:

𝟭. 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝘀. Check out sites like Acquire and WellFound to see what small startups and 1 person businesses are building for inspiration.

𝟮. 𝗗𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲. 𝗔𝗱𝗱 𝗮 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸. Check out the feature requests or reviews for an app you’re using. What do people want? Maybe build that.

𝟯. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗣𝗜 on rapidAPI or use OpenAI (everyone’s doing it 😎) and think what you can build around it. For example, can you scrape a user’s top posts as a way to train GPT on their voice and content?

𝟰. 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀. Is there something at work or in your personal life that you do manually that could be automated? Spreadsheets are an easy target. Fix it for yourself and others.

You also don’t need to solve anything. 

A great side project really only has 1 metric for success: you learned something.

Here's what we see working for students at Parsity:

Don't over-think it. Explain that you're genuinely excited for this opportunity and can't wait to start.

But...

You're hoping to move closer to [insert number here].

As long as that number is not laughably more than the offer, it's safe to ask.

I have NEVER, ever seen an offer pulled from 𝘁𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗳𝘂𝗹 negotiating.

I have a confession.

I've copy pasted throughout my entire coding career.

Honestly, it’s how I’ve survived over the years as a developer.

On every team where I worked, I took note of what the smarter developers were doing.

I copied from the right people at some amazing companies and worked with developers who I truly think might be genius.

I stole a little piece of each of these developers to accelerate my own career.

The lessons I learned from each of these characters saved me from mediocrity and might help you as well.

Listening to too many influencers on LinkedIn will get you stuck in a learning loop.

Goes a little something like this:

- Bald tech bro with a blue background tells you about hawt technology 🔥 (agree?)
- You, a little insecure about your own skills, thinks this is THE way to get noticed.
- You buy a course or a book or go down a YouTube rabbit hole.

Repeat this a few times and you will be a sub-par developer in many technologies instead of good at a couple.

Instead:

- Focus on your core skills and identify trends in the local and global market (hint: ReactJS ain’t going away)
- Resist the urge to add more tools to your tool belt early on
- Focus on getting interviews and learning from your failures or successes
- Use a side project to reinforce your current skills and incrementally add new technologies


Lastly, just join parsity.io/inner-circle, a mentorship program for career changers who want to break into tech.

It stung to hear that. He was also right.

I was not junior either. 

I had been using AngularJS for a couple years. (don't judge me) 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺: I’d become a framework developer. I knew how to use AngularJS but didn’t understand the JS or patterns behind it.

I resolved to suck less at JS.

I went back to the basics including:
 
- promises
- async/await
- 𝚝𝚑𝚒𝚜
- design patterns
- closure

I went through all the Kyle Simpson books. I made janky apps to internalize the information. I gained knowledge and confidence.

Understanding the fundamentals provides a lot of benefits:

- frameworks become less magical
- you start seeing patterns everywhere
- less learning curve when switching between technologies
- libraries become more read-able

Frameworks are great. You need to know them. Just don’t build your house on a shaky foundation.

There are developers with less talent than you who are getting hired. 

I know the news sucks right now but hear me out:

You are likely not competing for the same roles as the influx of highly paid engineers who just came into the market.

So continue to work on your skills, keep applying to all those non-sexy companies and tech-adjacent roles and make connections online and IRL.

Some will tell you that getting that your first role (or the next one) is a 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗲. Others will say 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀. 

Neither is wrong. 

Try a combination and do what works for you.

𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗗𝗠 𝗺𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗜'𝗹𝗹 𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗸 𝟭 𝗼𝗿 𝟮 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗽!

Here’s the harsh truth about interviews that no one ever really addresses:

Luck is a factor.

You could be absolutely qualified for a position and study all the relevant material.

Get a bad interviewer? All that pre-work might go down the drain.

Maybe your interviewer asks a crazy difficult question or has different standards for what constitutes a reasonable solution? 

Or maybe luck works in your favor.

Maybe you study a particular question that you have memorized and then you get asked that question.

Maybe the interview is not technical at all and just consists of small talk and personality fit.

So if you’ve recently bombed an interview or are beating yourself up because you see others achieving success on a timeline that doesn’t seem possible for you, realize that interviewers are both a game of skill AND chance.

Increase your surface area for luck by continuing to apply, studying and separating signals from noise.

Pro-tip: Don’t.

Here’s how I approach it:

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟭: 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 - duh 🙄

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯: 𝗕𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 - update that core component from the previous step by adding a line of code or removing a line. What breaks? Why?

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟰: 𝗙𝗶𝘅 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 - extend the component by adding more data to the API response or changing the color of a button.

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟱: 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗮 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 - this can be time consuming but will force you to understand the feature you're poking at. At least read a few of the tests to see what the intention of the code is.

Lastly - realize that it can take months to feel comfortable in a new codebase. 

𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗶𝗻 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀. Ask why things work the way they do and repeat steps 1 - 5 as needed.

Well this is it, I’m getting fired.

The engineering manager and I were sitting in a small room, frantically trying to fix a program I had released to production that was breaking spectacularly.

The code was on a large monitor for us investigate.

“What is this code supposed to do?” he asked.

I froze.

- First, Chat Gippity took your job.
- Next, Devin AI made programming obsolete.
- Applications to McDonald's skyrocketed. Mostly CS grads.
- All hiring stopped in software. A total of 0 positions opened up.

- The Devin team hired devs made of flesh.
- Too many JS libraries were produced.
- 100% of companies talked about AI. Just 6.1% of businesses are using AI to produce their products or services (according to Goldman Sachs).

The big takeaway here:

Stop planning your career based on click bait.

How does it feel to be the worst developer on a team?

I had the unpleasant experience of holding this title when I worked at a small startup.

I had more technical growth in the short time I was there than at any other company I’ve worked since.

You’ve probably heard the advice “𝘐𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶’𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘮𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘰𝘰𝘮, 𝘪𝘵’𝘴 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘰𝘰𝘮.”

Easier said than done.

The guilt and anxiety I felt on a daily basis was difficult to deal with. I was confronted with my own limitations and the realization that 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗮𝘀𝗻’𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗶𝗻 𝗺𝘆 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱.

I could barely keep up with the tasks I was assigned and relied on lots of pairing sessions to get my work done.

I could either quit or at least attempt to keep up with the other devs and contribute to the best of my ability.

I made a resolution to suck less.

- I asked the smarty-pants devs what books they suggested I read
- I audited my Javascript knowledge and wrote out what I knew I had to learn to contribute to discussions
- enrolled in a course to learn DSA and comp sci fundamentals
- someone made a joke about Djikstra… who the hell is that? I would find out

I never became the 2nd worst developer at this company, but I grew my technical skills, confidence and threshold for failure.

As uncomfortable as it was, I know see just how pivotal this experience was.

So if you’re just starting out, or maybe on a new team and discovering just how little you know…good. Embrace the suck, expose your ignorance and be prepared to learn.

My favorite mental models for computer science concepts:

𝗥𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 - Russian dolls: Each doll holds another, representing a function calling itself.

𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗟𝗶𝘀𝘁𝘀 - Train cars: Each train car is linked to the next, just like each node points to the next node in a linked list.

𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘀 - Stack of plates: You can only take from the top or add to the top, similar to how a stack operates (Last-In, First-Out).

𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘂𝗲𝘀 - Line to get on a bus: First person in line is first to get on, which represents the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle.

𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗲𝘀 - Family tree: Each “parent” node has “child” nodes, and the child can also be a parent with children.

𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗢 𝗡𝗼𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 - Traffic on a highway: As more cars (inputs) join, the effect on speed varies depending on the road’s capacity (algorithm’s efficiency).

- focus on recursion and backtracking after learning trees (𝘐 𝘧𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘪𝘵 𝘮𝘢𝘥𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘯𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘺)
- time yourself solving LC problems - shoot for 30 mins for medium problems and write the space and time complexity next to your solution
- learn common approaches to optimize algorithms (𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘩𝘮𝘢𝘱𝘴, 𝘮𝘦𝘮𝘰𝘪𝘻𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯...)

Just because MAANG exclusively asks DSA, the majority of your interviews as a front end developer will probably be on a combination of:

- behavioral and technical assessments  
- challenges that involve string manipulation and working with arrays && objects
- JS trivia  (explain closure 🙄)
- building small components using ReactJS

❌ Get a job you love and you’ll never work a day in your life.

Look, I love to write code and mentor people.

But there’s so much more to software development than writing code and pair-programming.

Some of the non-sexy stuff you’ll do as a developer:


- meetings
- on-call shifts
- writing documentation
- maintaining legacy code
- meetings to prepare for other meetings
- translating technical limitations to non-coders
- researching poorly documented 3rd party APIs

Coding is my hobby and profession. It’s a job and I try not to wrap too much of my identity into it.

Let me make this very simple for you:

- Build an app you might actually find useful and deploy it.
- Connect with people who show interest.

Walk down main street and see what business has an awful website they need re-done.

Let's call him Don.

First off, this guy was a genius.

I could tell because when we went out to eat on the first day of work with the CEO and CTO - this guy used his hands to eat a salad.

Next, he asked if he could go home early because he was tired.

He slept on the couch in the office in the middle of the day.

Only a genius can get away with shit like that and not get fired on the spot.

I was entering my 3rd year as a developer and thought of myself as mid-level at this point.

Wrong.

Don pair-programmed with me for the first 2 weeks on the job and I quickly learned just how junior I was.

Don wrote tests for the features we created using the library he authored for the framework we were using.

We only worked together for 9 months but I can't think of a more impactful stint in my career. I learned the art of testing, the importance of learning your tools and how to balance getting things done with getting them done correctly.

I bet he's still eating salad with his hands.

Can we all agree that snapshot tests are pointless 99% of the time?

They somehow sneak into our test suites with good intentions.

Inevitably they result in false alarms and are ignored.

Unit tests are concerned with confirming expected functionality. We make sure that clicking a button actually results in an event happening for example.

Now we have these pesky snapshots.

They take a pic (a snapshot if you will) of the DOM output and then compare the original code to the current output. If there’s a difference, we get a failed test.

Maybe you changed the button color from light-green to not-so-light green.

Whoops.

Used incorrectly, snapshots give us a false sense of security or get ignored entirely. 

They contribute to vanity test coverage metrics with no real benefit.

Am I way off base here? If you’ve used snapshots in a useful way I’d love to hear about it.

I’m not optimistic because I’m foolish or naive.

I’m optimistic because it’s the most practical strategy I’ve found to get through life and create luck.

The photo below is me 4 years ago, getting taken to the hospital in an ambulance on the second day of my new job with a heart condition.

I didn’t know if I would come home so I wanted my last picture to be me smiling.

I had done all the right things: 

- Quit alcohol
- Had an exercise routine
- Lost weight
- Wrote tests for my code even when I didn’t have to

And yet here I was - maybe about to die.

Plot twist: I Iived!

Could it happen again? 

Sure.

I have a couple options:

1. Stress everyday, take a bunch of heart pills and avoid strenuous activity
2. Resume life

I choose option 2. 

Your brain is a pattern-finding wizard. It will find “evidence” to support your assumptions.

Start looking for proof that things can and will get better and that life tends to incrementally improve and you aren’t the unluckiest person you know.

For me, this means limiting local news and social media and generally not hanging around people who always have drama and unfollowing accounts who push fear.

Junior developers are inherently risky (in every industry, not just tech btw).

"𝘉𝘶𝘵... 𝘐 𝘢𝘮 𝘢 𝘫𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘰𝘳", you say.

Yeah, I get it, I get it, just bare with me here.

The word "junior" is so subjective that it's nearly meaningless. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗼𝗶𝗹𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝘀𝗼 𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 𝗻𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗼𝘄𝗻.

• They need significant hand-holding for months on the job.
• They will take on the easy stuff and maybe break some things.
• They won't contribute much.

𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴: nearly every developer will be "junior" when they first join a company unless they are very senior.

You don't actually need to a be a mid level developer to be a safe hire. You just need to avoid the tell-tale signs that you are, in fact, a n00b.

Quite simply, stop down-playing yourself.

• 𝗥𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗷𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗿, 𝗮𝘀𝗽𝗶𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 from your resume and LinkedIn.
• DON'T talk about "the project from your school or bootcamp"
• 𝗗𝗢 𝗧𝗮𝗹𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽 𝗼𝗿 𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 - yes, you need to have a project to talk about.
• 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 and speak to the benefits of features you created. 
• Instead of "created a full stack app with a laundry list of tech" try "migrated a JS app to Typescript to improve developer experience and velocity".

You ever feel like you’re basically coding the same few features over and over and over?

Sometimes your current role doesn’t prepare you for the next role.

Recipe for terrible 1 on 1’s:

Manager: “Anything to discuss this week?”

You: “Nah, I’m chilling”

Manager: “Nice. Talk to ya next time 👍”

1 on 1’s can devolve into weekly status updates, which is why I think a lot of people like to skip them. 

I asked 3 engineering leaders how have 1 on 1’s that don’t suck:

Nick Cosentino 👇

What you can do is talk about:

- 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗶𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴
- 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲/𝗻𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 with peers and partner teams so I can help offer guidance or follow up
- 𝗥𝗼𝗮𝗱𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝘀, whether they are technical or with people
- 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝘀𝗽𝗶𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 and whether or not you feel we’re aligned on career progression
- Your level of motivation, engagement, excitement, interest, learning opportunity etc… on your current project

This time is about YOU and as much as I would love to lead the charge on all of these things: You should take responsibility to do this as well.

Ken Corey 👇

Your plans, your dreams, your challenges, where you can improve.

- Talk about 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗴𝗼𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻, as well as your goals outside the career plan.
- Talk about how to progress (𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗱𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸).
- Talk about 𝘂𝗽𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀.
- Talk about challenges.
- Talk about managing up. Not all TL/EMs are comfortable with these meetings.

John Crickett 👇

Shocking and not so shocking takeaways from the 2024 Stack Overflow Developer Survey:

1. Javascript is STILL the most popular programming language - take that haters
2. 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗩𝗦 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 - learn it like a pro.
3. Bootcamps love MERN - 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗡. There’s never been a better time to learn SQL with offerings like Supabase that make it too easy to start.
4. 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁 𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴? With ReactJS on the server and the popularity of NextJS does this mean more people identify as full stack? 
5. 𝗙𝗲𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗷𝗼𝗯𝘀 than last year. A significantly higher percentage of students and people learning to code do see it as a threat.

What does it all mean?

There are entire books written on the magical art of estimation for software projects.

𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗜'𝘃𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗸 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀:

1. 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗯-𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀 needed for delivery of a feature and 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗳 𝗱𝗮𝘆𝘀 for all tasks. This includes things like styling.
   
2. Each day, 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗮𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘂𝗯 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀 and see if you're on track or not.

3. Write the actual time next to your original estimation.

4. At the end of the project 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗱𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀.

How old is too old to learn to code?

According to the internet, that age is 40.

I think that's silly.

I am fully aware that bias exists. Humans are... human. I also know that in the last 10 years, I've worked with amazing developers of all ages. On my first team, a couple of the devs were over 70. At a small startup in San Francisco, our senior was in his mid-50's.

I can't imagine living life based on taking the safest path. It would not only be boring but wildly unfulfilling.

The reality of the advice you read on social media:

Nearly all of it will work, but not necessarily for you.

Here’s how you cut through the noise to pick out the gems in a sea of trash:

- Has the person achieved the outcome you want?
- Do you have anything in common with this person?
- Do they seem happy?

If the answer to all 3 is NO, maybe don’t take their advice.

4. 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀. Is there something at work or in your personal life that you do manually that could be automated? Spreadsheets are an easy target. Fix it for yourself and others.

Honestly, it’s how I’ve survived over the years as a developer.

Every new workplace where I went and every contract I completed, I took note of what the smarter developers were doing.

- what books had they read?
- I read their pull requests, even when I wasn’t the reviewer.
- I copied their styles for writing tests, React components and backend code.
- I asked how they investigated and debugged critical issues.
- I imitated their mannerisms and studied how they spoke in meetings.

I’ve been lucky. I copied from the right people at some amazing companies and worked with developers who I truly think might be genius.

You don’t have to get lucky though.

Nowadays, through LinkedIn, open source and the University of YouTube, you have the ability to learn from other amazing developers and copy what makes sense to you.

The job search can feel unrewarding, draining and shake what little confidence you have in yourself.

It’s a game of both skill and chance.

You can be absolutely qualified and still “fail”.

Rejection is rarely personal, it’s an inevitable consequence of many factors:

- 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 (ask 5 people to look at your resume and get 5 different opinions)

- Some 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 but open roles to the public with 0 intention of hiring

- 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 in favor of a specific answer even when presented with working (or even better) alternatives

So what does this mean?

- Expect failure and learn from it.
- Try your hardest not to take it personally.

Whatever you do, please do not stop playing the game.

You only have to win once.

The problem with 99% of the technical interview advice you read is that it applies to the top 1% of companies out there.

I spoke with over 500 developers in the last couple years and now own an online coding school, Parsity where we’ve rolled out mock interviews which reflect the reality of the non-tech job market.

𝗛𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝟰 𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀 𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿-𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘄𝗲𝗯 𝗱𝗲𝘃 𝗿𝗼𝗹𝗲𝘀:

- build a React component that fetches data
- JS trivia including closure, 𝚕𝚎𝚝 vs 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚜𝚝, event loop and 𝚝𝚑𝚒𝚜
- take home assignment that’s supposed to take 2 hours but is really a full day 😅
- code challenges using 2 pointers, sliding window and array manipulation

I’ve also met developers who accepted offers after no technical screening at all! This has happened to me at least twice.

While you’re pounding LeetCode, don’t forget to have some answers in your back pocket for questions like “𝘵𝘦𝘭𝘭 𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘴𝘦𝘭𝘧?” or “𝘸𝘩𝘺 𝘥𝘰 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦?”

1. 𝗕𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀: Between coding challenges and take home assignments, I prepared a list of technical stories from my work experience, to answer the most common behavioral questions that I've been asked over and over again.
   
2. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗺𝘆𝘁𝗵. Our entire org got axed at a big, stable, non-tech company. There is no where to hide nowadays. Tech is not the only industry affected by layoffs and economic instability.

My poor Git skills didn't really bite me until 3 years into my career.

I had just been hired as a developer for a cool tech startup. I volunteered to handle a code release, just like I've recommended in previous posts. 

The lead developer was off that night and told me his process to merge a small change from one branch to production.

Simple, I thought.

He scribbled his Git work flow on a whiteboard in a small office while I tried to hide my anxiety. It was so much different than any flow I'd used. 𝗜 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗱𝗺𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘁.

I wrote down the process step by step in my notebook as if it was some secret spell.

That night I merged something into production successfully.

One problem:

It wasn't the right code 😬.

My manager saved me that morning and we reverted my changes and merged the correct code.

I was painfully embarrassed. I also knew it was time for me to actually understand how to use Git.

Here are a few things which helped me get Git before I got got... 🧐

- use 𝚘𝚑𝚖𝚢𝚣𝚜𝚑 to 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗺𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗚𝗶𝘁-𝗳𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗹𝘆
- 𝗮𝗱𝗱 𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗮𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 so I could type things like 𝚐𝚌𝚘 instead of 𝚐𝚒𝚝 𝚌𝚑𝚎𝚌𝚔𝚘𝚞𝚝
- learn how to 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 within a branch with 𝚐𝚒𝚝 𝚕𝚘𝚐
- 𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗺𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀 to see where I introduced a bug using 𝚐𝚒𝚝 𝚋𝚒𝚜𝚎𝚌𝚝
- 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮 𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 on a different branch 𝚐𝚒𝚝 𝚌𝚑𝚎𝚌𝚔𝚘𝚞𝚝 <𝚋𝚛𝚊𝚗𝚌𝚑> -- 𝚙𝚊𝚝𝚑/𝚝𝚘/𝚏𝚒𝚕𝚎
- understand how to 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁 𝚐𝚒𝚝 𝚛𝚎𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚝 <𝚌𝚘𝚖𝚖𝚒𝚝-𝚑𝚊𝚜𝚑-𝚏𝚛𝚘𝚖-𝚘𝚛𝚒𝚐𝚒𝚗𝚊𝚕-𝚛𝚎𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚝>
- 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘀 into a branch with 𝚌𝚑𝚎𝚛𝚛𝚢-𝚙𝚒𝚌𝚔

My major flaw is that I was too concerned with memorizing a particular set of commands to achieve something. There are at 𝚗 different ways to get the same outcome with Git.

I now like to start with a simple question: "𝘞𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘮 𝘐 𝘵𝘳𝘺𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘰?" and work backwards from there.

Could there be a worse time to learn to code?

I was 2 months sober, working a full time job while doing ride share on the side and had 2 kids at home.

I had negative time.

𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝟮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿: time management.

It really just boiled down to:

1. 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼 (𝘦𝘹: 𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘳𝘰𝘸 - 𝘧𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘩 𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 1 𝘰𝘧 Colt Steele'𝘴 𝘜𝘥𝘦𝘮𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘴𝘦)

I resolved to become the best damn code reviewer on the team that day.

A year later, during my annual review, my manager told me that my peers were complimenting my reviews. I had prevented errors from slipping through and suggested solutions which led to more maintainable code.

𝗜 𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴:

1. Block off time in the morning to do the review
2. Understand the work being done by reading the ticket associated with the PR
3. Run code locally before looking at the code
4. Read the code and ask questions or suggest improvements
5. Use Loom or a screen share to discuss details or schedule a pair session if needed

Your manager isn't some sadistic bastard. In most cases at least. The reason they didn't confront you or offer feedback is because they are human. They just want to focus on their work and avoid conflict.

On day 1, you should set some practical milestones with your team lead or manager. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 in the first month or two on the job?

For a junior developer it might look like this:

𝗗𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝟭 - 𝟯𝟬: Get all repos running locally on your machine and understand code review and deployment processes. Get at least 2 small features into production.

𝗗𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝟯𝟬 - 𝟲𝟬: Participate in an on-call rotation and learn process for critical incidents. Understand the full software development lifecycle. Be able to fix small bugs with little help.

𝗗𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝟲𝟬 - 𝟵𝟬: Take on a mid-level difficulty feature and deploy to production. Contribute to technical discussions.

Once you're aligned on what success looks like, it's no longer a guessing game and you have proof that you are where you should be or have an idea about where you need to improve.

I’ve gained quite a lot more followers on here so I figure it’s time to out myself again:

12 years ago I was addicted to drinking and drugs and living a criminal lifestyle.

After an intervention, I promised to quit, unsure if I would actually be able to do it for more than a week (10 years later and I’m going strong 💪)

I noticed I had a lot of time on my hands now with none of my terrible outlets available.

I found Codecademy.com and wrote my first line of code. I was hooked (notice a theme here?)

Kept building stuff.

Sucked less each year.

Obviously you have to want to change. You need desire and most importantly, direction. 

Here’s what worked for me:

- exercising daily

- finding a replacement relapse when triggered (e.g. I eat a ton of sweets when I want to do… other stuff)

- find a hobby to fill in the time (for me it was coding, for you maybe reading or puzzles)

- schedule events on days you would normally do stupid things (I watched a ton of awful movies on Thursday and Friday nights in movie theaters to pass the time)

- tell everyone you quit - you’ll feel a lot more embarrassed if you fail and therefore incentivized to succeed

I sincerely hope that helps.

What’s your tips for people just starting a new dev position?

Quintessential junior dev move:

Wasting hours solving a problem a co-worker could’ve helped you figure out in minutes.

No, this is not a long term solution to becoming an effective developer.

Also:

You are ultimately judged on the work you complete. When you bump your head against your technical depth, acknowledge it and ask for help.

But for Jeebus sake please don’t just say “I can’t figure out [𝘹]”

Try this:

- I’m having an issue with [𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘧𝘪𝘤 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘣𝘭𝘦𝘮]
- I’ve tried [𝘺] but it’s not working in the way I expect which is [𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘺]

- Is anyone available to take a look with me sometime today or point me in the right direction?

Don’t let your ego get in the way of progress.

There’s too much to learn.

- A new framework to replace the old one that you just learned.
- Obscure algorithms from dudes with too many letters in their last name.
- Everyone is switching to AI/ML now? Should you learn Python?

While you can’t JUST stick to the basics, if you chase every shiny new technology you will become a Swiss Army Knife developer. You can do a little of everything… poorly.

Instead, identify mega vs micro trends in software development:

- Recent mega trends include K8s, NextJS, Serverless and TypeScript.
- Micro trends might include tRPC, edge computing and PWA. 
- Use side projects to gain experience with technologies that make up mega trends and keep your skills relevant. 

Gamble a bit with the micro trends. 

If you’re lucky, some of them will become mega trends and you’ll be first in line to take advantage.

𝗚𝗿𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝗹𝗶𝗻e. The surest way towards failure is to quit. Most people will choose this route.

If you find yourself in a cycle of hard work but low performance, take a step back and evaluate. 

You might just find that a slight change in approach can lead to significant improvements.

There is a valuable skill that will set you apart from most developers. It will go from a nice to have to a requirement if you want to move into leadership:

Public speaking.

If you’re like me, maybe you think you can just hide in your code hole and never speak.

I tried this method for a few years and it sorta worked.

I didn’t get fired. 

I also couldn’t get promoted or make much of an impact.

Now, as an engineering manager, my job is a lot of coding but it’s also a lot of speaking. To get over my fear I did a few things:

1. Write down questions to ask during meetings 
2. Volunteer for a lunch and learn
3. Explain my code over a video using Loom (I made so many videos I’ve never shared)
4. Make a commitment to be the first to break the silence in a meeting - even with a dumb question (see #1)

You’re probably your worst critic. 

We’re all much too wrapped up in ourselves to remember the dumb thing you said in that meeting last Tuesday.

Turn off the tutorial. 

Open the code editor.

You’re going to learn a hell of a lot more from:

- getting stuck
- reading the documentation
- realizing the docs suck
- getting rate limited on Chat GPT
- throwing everything at the wall
- finally figuring it out
- feeling like a genius… for a few minutes

as opposed to:

- typing what another person has typed

1. Not learning the fundamentals before diving into frameworks
2. Refusing to admit when I didn’t know something
3. Only taking on tasks I knew I could finish
4. Not understanding how engineering relates to business goals
